notes:
I've written notes for every verse except v. 3's Joah and v. 17 beyond the exile point. I didn't find any Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity-teaching material on this chapter, so those are left out. I found no clear split between Protestant traditions, but commentators do disagree on a few points, and I've marked those **[Disagreement]**.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) dates this to about 700 BC under the godly King Hezekiah. He notes the same events are told in 2 Kings 18 and 2 Chronicles 32. He also sees the fall of Judah's cities as fulfilling Isaiah's earlier prophecies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/
- The Pulpit Commentary says that, by Sennacherib's own account, his 701 BC campaign "captured forty-six of the strong cities" belonging to Hezekiah. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/36-1.htm
- Constable thinks Isaiah leaves out Hezekiah's attempt to buy Sennacherib off (2 Kings 18:13-16) probably because he wanted to focus on the Judean king's good example of trusting God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html
- **[Disagreement — the date]** Ellicott reports that nearly all the Assyrian scholars of his day thought the chronology needed correcting. Sennacherib's inscriptions put the campaign in Hezekiah's 27th year, not his 14th. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm Dummelow suggests the date originally applied to Isaiah 38 (Hezekiah's illness), worked out from the 15 extra years Hezekiah was given. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/isaiah-36.html
- Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey): Scholars date Hezekiah's reign to either ca. 727-698 BCE or ca. 715-686 BCE. Some explain these differing dates by postulating a coregency. https://uploads.bibleodyssey.org/articles/hezekiah/ Hezekiah led an anti-Assyrian coalition, and after Judah's fortified cities fell Hezekiah capitulated (2Kgs 18:14-16). https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/sennacherib/

**v. 2**
- "Rabshakeh" is a title, not a name. Ellicott takes it as probably "chief officer or cup-bearer." The Cambridge Bible gives the Assyrian *Rab-saq*, "chief of the officers." Gill and Barnes explain that the Tartan and Rabsaris came too (2 Kings 18:17), but Rabshakeh is named because he did the talking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-2.htm
- Ellicott says Sennacherib took Hezekiah's huge payment and then tore up the treaty, sending his officers to demand an unconditional surrender. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
- On the place where he stood:
  - Ellicott: it was the same spot where Isaiah had confronted Ahaz (Isa 7:3). It was probably chosen by the Rabshakeh as commanding one end of the aqueduct which supplied the city with water. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-2.htm
  - Beall (in Precept Austin) sees a deliberate contrast between Hezekiah and his father Ahaz. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
  - Kingcomments says the Holy Spirit is reminding us of Hezekiah's faith set against Ahaz's unbelief. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/isaiah-36.html
- Gill says the pool was just outside the walls, which shows the envoy's daring. He reports a Jewish view that Rabshakeh was an apostate Jew, and some who claimed he was Isaiah's son. Gill calls that second claim without any foundation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-2.htm Calvin's notes also record the apostate-Jew view and call it "not altogether improbable." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html
- **[Disagreement — one campaign or two?]** The Pulpit Commentary argues this mission was a separate, later expedition after a fresh provocation, likely Hezekiah's appeal to Egypt. It notes the Assyrian annals, which never record any reverse or defeat, are wholly silent as to this second expedition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-2.htm The Layman's Bible Commentary also discusses the two-campaign theory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/isaiah-36.html
- Guzik mentions the Lachish relief in the British Museum and a pit at Lachish holding about 1,500 dead from the siege. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/

**v. 3**
- Ellicott sees it as significant that Eliakim now holds the office Shebna once held, while Shebna has been demoted to scribe (Isa 22:15-25). He credits the change to Isaiah's influence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm Constable says some think this fulfils Isaiah 22:20-23. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html

**v. 4**
- Rabshakeh doesn't call Hezekiah "king." Meanwhile "the great king" was the Assyrian rulers' own boastful title (Constable; Keil and Delitzsch). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-4.htm
- Precept Austin calls this a great question from a pagan king, and pictures the Holy Spirit stirring Hezekiah's heart through it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
- Guzik sees Rabshakeh's whole speech as a psychological attack on every source of hope Judah had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/

**v. 5**
- A NET note (quoted in Precept Austin) says the message appears to be in broken Hebrew at this point. "Word of lips" means empty talk, as in Proverbs 14:23. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
- Calvin reads it as irony, as though Rabshakeh were saying, "I see what you're thinking, but it's just talk." He notes the verse is explained in various ways. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Rabshakeh is right that Isaiah warned against trusting Egypt. But he says it to drive Judah to despair, not to God. Guzik compares this to how Satan uses truth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/
- Ellicott: news of Hezekiah's dealings with Egypt had reached Assyria. Sennacherib's own inscriptions say the Egyptian king could not save those who trusted him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
- **[Disagreement — did Hezekiah really trust Egypt?]**
  - Calvin (Reformed) says Rabshakeh slanderously and falsely accuses the pious king. Yet God let this happen to rebuke a people who had ignored Isaiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html
  - J. Vernon McGee says Hezekiah *was* looking to Egypt, so on that point Rabshakeh was accurate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/36-14.html
  - Guzik, in his 2 Kings 18 commentary, says Hezekiah put his hope in the Egyptian alliance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-18/
  - Kingcomments says the alliance was made by the responsible leaders, not Hezekiah himself, though as king he was ultimately answerable. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/isaiah-36.html
  - Ligonier calls Rabshakeh's warning about Egypt "actually good advice." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/assyria-invades-judah

**v. 7**
- The traditional reading is unanimous: Rabshakeh misunderstood Hezekiah's reform.
  - Ellicott: in Assyrian thinking, a god was honoured by having more shrines. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
  - MacArthur (in Precept Austin): worship centred on one temple was "utterly foreign" to polytheists. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
  - Constable: Hezekiah was really purifying the worship of Yahweh. Constable adds that many Judeans may have resented the reform, and Rabshakeh was appealing to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html
  - Keil and Delitzsch call the argument both heathen and "very crafty." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-4.htm
- Guzik: the high places broke Leviticus 17. He applies the verse against do-it-yourself religion (Bellah's "Sheilaism"). He also quotes Grogan, who argues the theological mistake actually supports the speech being authentic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/
- Matthew Henry turns the verse into a warning to "presuming sinners" who claim to trust in God's mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/36-2.html
- Ligonier says the passage gives "remarkable insight into Assyrian theology." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/Sennacherib-Defeated

**v. 8**
- Ellicott translates "make a wager," and calls it a taunt Rabshakeh added to the official message. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm Parker also reads it as a wager. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/isaiah-36.html
- Guzik: Rabshakeh's real goal is to get Judah to give up without a fight. Satan does the same, as in the temptation of Jesus (Luke 4:5-8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/

**v. 9**
- Keil and Delitzsch: Assyria was feared above all for its cavalry and chariots. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-4.htm
- Utley: the sarcasm is that Jerusalem couldn't even beat a local militia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/isaiah-36.html

**v. 10**
- **[Disagreement — how much truth is in "The LORD said to me"?]**
  - Guzik: the claim was "partially true," since Assyria was fulfilling God's prophesied plan. But God didn't tempt an innocent man, and Assyria can't use this as an excuse, any more than Judas could. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/
  - Ellicott gives three options: an empty boast; Isaiah's teaching had become known; or Sennacherib claimed a dream. He notes Sennacherib's inscriptions regularly claim divine backing for his wars. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
  - Matthew Henry: Rabshakeh had really come up *against* the Lord (Isa 37:28). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/36-2.html
  - Parker calls it "a perverted truth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/isaiah-36.html
  - Kingcomments: perhaps he had heard of Isaiah 10:5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/isaiah-36.html
  - A NET note (in Precept Austin) says he claims the Lord has made Assyria his tool of discipline. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary

**v. 11**
- Aramaic was the language of diplomacy. Ordinary people in Palestine didn't speak it until much later (Constable). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html
- Ellicott suggests the officials feared the people would hear an echo of Isaiah's warnings and lose heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott calls the words unmatched in their "brutal coarseness." They imply Assyria could cut off both food and water. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
- Calvin: Rabshakeh speaks like a conqueror, treating Hezekiah as a slave. He wants unconditional surrender, not terms. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html
- Constable: the aim was to split the people from their king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: he stood up to get attention and deliberately raised his voice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/36-13.htm
- Precept Austin calls it "calculated intimidation." It points to Psalm 47:2: the LORD is the true Great King. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary

**v. 14**
- Calvin: it is true that Hezekiah couldn't save them without God. But Hezekiah never claimed he could. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html
- Utley (in Precept Austin): the verb "deceive" is the one used of the serpent deceiving Eve (Gen 3:13). https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
- Guzik: the aim was to make the people doubt their leaders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: Rabshakeh had probably heard of Hezekiah's speech in 2 Chronicles 32:7-8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
- Constable: the Assyrians apparently knew Isaiah's policy of trusting God was popular. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html
- Calvin: Rabshakeh sets an "uncertain" hope against benefits in hand. Satan uses the same trick against believers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html

**v. 16**
- JFB: "make peace" is literally "blessing." https://biblehub.com/library/jamieson/commentary_critical_and_explanatory_on_the_whole_bible/isa_36_1-22_sennacheribs_invasion_blasphemous.htm
- Calvin: the real comparison is between God and the king of Assyria. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html
- Precept Austin calls this a deceptive offer: destruction dressed up as opportunity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary

**v. 17**
- Several commentators make the same point: exile is being sold as an improvement.
  - Parker and Ellicott say he offers exile as if it were a change for the better. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/isaiah-36.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
  - JFB: he is softening the known Assyrian policy of deporting conquered peoples. https://biblehub.com/library/jamieson/commentary_critical_and_explanatory_on_the_whole_bible/isa_36_1-22_sennacheribs_invasion_blasphemous.htm
  - Guzik: he glosses over forced resettlement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/
- Calvin sees in this verse a picture of Satan's daily temptation: pulling us from trusting God through the world's comforts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: this is the natural speech of polytheism. The LORD is treated as one national god among many. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
- Calvin: lumping God in with idols is a special kind of blasphemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html
- Guzik: Rabshakeh overplays his hand here and seals his fate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: by Assyrian practice, the answer to "where are the gods?" was literal: they sat in Assyria's temples as trophies. He also identifies Sepharvaim with Sippara. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm

**v. 20**
- Constable: this states the choice the whole first half of Isaiah has posed. Can Yahweh save those who simply trust him, or is he no better than other gods? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-36.html
- Oswalt (in Precept Austin): chapters 7–39 explore whether God can be trusted, and here Sennacherib claims to be more trustworthy than God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary

**v. 21**
- **[Disagreement — the reason for the silence]**
  - Guzik: wise silence. Arguing with demonic logic is useless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-36/
  - Precept Austin: restraint and trust that the battle is the Lord's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
  - Ellicott: Hezekiah may not have trusted his envoys' judgment, since their only words so far (v. 11) had made matters worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: tearing their clothes showed horror at blasphemy (compare Matthew 26:65). It was also a silent protest aimed at the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/36.htm
- Precept Austin: grief over the dishonour done to God, and humility as they seek his help. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-36-commentary
- Calvin's notes suggest torn clothes may point to the blasphemer being an Israelite. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-36.html

---

**Notes on traditions and gaps**
- **No real denominational split.** The disagreements above split individual commentators, not traditions. For reference, the traditions represented are:
  - Reformed: Calvin, Ligonier
  - Baptist: Gill
  - Methodist: Wesley
  - Enduring Word: Guzik
- **Wesley's notes** only summarise the chapter. Rabshakeh by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt, and the story is included to explain and confirm some of the foregoing predictions. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-isaiah/
- **Left out:**
  - Catholic and Orthodox commentary (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org): I found none on this chapter.
  - Prosperity, word-of-faith and hyper-grace treatments: I found none.
  - Full Gill and Pulpit notes for each verse: I only read them for v. 2. I also didn't read the NET notes directly, only as quoted on Precept Austin.
